verses.text: Now in the eighteenth year of king Jeroboam the son of Nebat, Abijam began to reign over Judah.
He reigned three years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Maacah the daughter of Abishalom.
He walked in all the sins of his father, which he had done before him; and his heart was not perfect with Yahweh his God, as the heart of David his father.
Nevertheless for David’s sake, Yahweh his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem, to set up his son after him, and to establish Jerusalem;
because David did that which was right in Yahweh’s eyes, and didn’t turn aside from anything that he commanded him all the days of his life, except only in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.
Now there was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all the days of his life.
The rest of the acts of Abijam, and all that he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah? There was war between Abijam and Jeroboam.
Abijam slept with his fathers, and they buried him in David’s city; and Asa his son reigned in his place.
In the twentieth year of Jeroboam king of Israel, Asa began to reign over Judah.
He reigned forty-one years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Maacah the daughter of Abishalom.
Asa did that which was right in Yahweh’s eyes, as David his father did.
He put away the sodomites out of the land, and removed all the idols that his fathers had made.
He also removed Maacah his mother from being queen, because she had made an abominable image for an Asherah. Asa cut down her image and burned it at the brook Kidron.
But the high places were not taken away. Nevertheless the heart of Asa was perfect with Yahweh all his days.
He brought into Yahweh’s house the things that his father had dedicated, and the things that he himself had dedicated: silver, gold, and utensils.
There was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days.
Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah, and built Ramah, that he might not allow anyone to go out or come in to Asa king of Judah.

Then Asa took all the silver and the gold that was left in the treasures of Yahweh’s house, and the treasures of the king’s house, and delivered it into the hand of his servants. Then King Asa sent them to Ben Hadad, the son of Tabrimmon, the son of Hezion, king of Syria, who lived at Damascus, saying,

“There is a treaty between me and you, between my father and your father. Behold, I have sent to you a present of silver and gold. Go, break your treaty with Baasha king of Israel, that he may depart from me.”
Ben Hadad listened to king Asa, and sent the captains of his armies against the cities of Israel, and struck Ijon, and Dan, and Abel Beth Maacah, and all Chinneroth, with all the land of Naphtali.
When Baasha heard of it, he stopped building Ramah, and lived in Tirzah.

Then king Asa made a proclamation to all Judah. No one was exempted. They carried away the stones of Ramah, and its timber, with which Baasha had built; and king Asa used it to build Geba of Benjamin, and Mizpah.

Now the rest of all the acts of Asa, and all his might, and all that he did, and the cities which he built, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah? But in the time of his old age he was diseased in his feet.
Asa slept with his fathers, and was buried with his fathers in his father David’s city; and Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his place.
Nadab the son of Jeroboam began to reign over Israel in the second year of Asa king of Judah; and he reigned over Israel two years.
He did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, and walked in the way of his father, and in his sin with which he made Israel to sin.
Baasha the son of Ahijah, of the house of Issachar, conspired against him; and Baasha struck him at Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines; for Nadab and all Israel were besieging Gibbethon.
Even in the third year of Asa king of Judah, Baasha killed him, and reigned in his place.

As soon as he was king, he struck all the house of Jeroboam. He didn’t leave to Jeroboam any who breathed, until he had destroyed him; according to the saying of Yahweh, which he spoke by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite;
for the sins of Jeroboam which he sinned, and with which he made Israel to sin, because of his provocation with which he provoked Yahweh, the God of Israel, to anger.
Now the rest of the acts of Nadab, and all that he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
There was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days.
In the third year of Asa king of Judah, Baasha the son of Ahijah began to reign over all Israel in Tirzah for twenty-four years.
He did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, and walked in the way of Jeroboam, and in his sin with which he made Israel to sin.

footnotes.content: Here begins the story of Abijam—notice how a king's reign is reckoned by another king's years. The kingdom remains, though it divides. There's something humbling in how the Lord lets both lines continue, keeping covenant even when His people do not.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three years—a short reign, but long enough to matter. Maacah appears here as mother; she returns again in later verses. Family shapes a kingdom more than we admit, sometimes for good, sometimes not.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He walked in his father's sins—not his own yet, but inherited them. How easy it is to step into the path made by those we love, especially when no one calls us back to the Lord. This is why faithfulness in one generation matters so much for the next.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: For David's sake—this is the lamp. Yahweh keeps His covenant with David, not because Abijam deserves it, but because the Lord's promises hold even when His kings do not. David himself wrote of this grace; here we see it lived out.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David did what was right, except in Uriah's matter. Even the psalmist we most admire was not spared his stumbling—yet Yahweh's covenant with him stood. This mystery has comforted many a weary heart who thought one failure ended everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: War between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all the days of his life—constant conflict. The kingdom torn in two bore the weight of that division in every season. Sometimes the cost of foolishness stretches across generations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The rest of his acts—we are reminded that this record is selection, not completeness. What we do not know is as important as what we do; the fuller story belongs to the Lord alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abijam slept with his fathers—the quiet turn of phrase that marks a reign's end. He is buried in David's city, honoring the line. Then Asa comes, and something shifts. One king makes his exit; another begins to walk a different path.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Asa began to reign—the twentieth year of Jeroboam. The years keep turning, and a new king rises. Watch now: this one will be different. Sometimes the Lord grants us rulers who seek Him, and the whole land changes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Forty-one years—Asa will reign long. His mother is Maacah, same name as Abijam's mother. The same woman, perhaps, or her daughter—either way, family lingers. Asa must choose whether to honor or to set aside what she has done.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Asa did that which was right in Yahweh's eyes, as David his father did. Notice the text calls David his 'father' in spirit, not blood—a spiritual claim. Asa chooses to follow David's example. We become the sons and daughters of those whose hearts we mirror.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He put away the sodomites and removed the idols his fathers made. A radical cleaning: Asa does not hide from the sins of his forebears but addresses them. This is not harshness but mercy—he frees the land from what had enslaved it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He removed Maacah his mother from being queen because of her abominable image for Asherah. The Hebrew runs deep here: 'removed' is the same word used in the previous verse. Asa's faithfulness to the Lord costs him his mother's position. Love and faithfulness are not always soft.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The high places were not taken away, yet his heart was perfect with Yahweh. How honest this is—Asa did much, but not all. He was not a perfect reformer, yet his heart held steadfast to the Lord. Sometimes we fear our incompleteness disqualifies us; the text teaches otherwise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He brought into Yahweh's house what his father had dedicated, and what he himself had dedicated—silver, gold, and utensils. Asa honors both what was given before and what he adds now. He sees himself not as replacing the past but as part of a chain of offerings.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days. The kingdom's division still tears at both sides. Despite Asa's faithfulness, conflict continues. We do not earn peace with all enemies by our own righteousness—sometimes the Lord fights the battles only He can win.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Baasha went up and built Ramah to block passage to Asa. The town of Ramah sits on the border between north and south; its name means 'height.' Baasha fortifies it strategically to strangle Judah. Geography shapes the kingdom's struggles.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Then Asa took all the silver and gold left in Yahweh's house and his own treasures. Here is where Asa stumbles—not in ritual but in trust. He takes what was sacred and uses it to buy peace from Syria. The Lord was not consulted; the covenant was not sought.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Asa says to Ben Hadad, 'Break your treaty with Baasha.' He speaks as one lord to another, offering gold for betrayal. It works—but at what cost to the kingdom's gold, and to Asa's own witness of faith?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ben Hadad sent his captains against the cities of Israel—Ijon, Dan, Abel Beth Maacah. These are real places in Naphtali; the strategy is to strike deep into Israel's north. The names anchor this moment in lived geography, not fable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When Baasha heard of it, he stopped building Ramah and lived in Tirzah. The tactic worked—Baasha withdraws. But again: how often do we win battles by the world's means and lose something larger in ourselves?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Asa made a proclamation: all Judah carried away the stones and timber Baasha had built and used them to build Geba and Mizpah. The people rally to their king's vision. Sometimes a leader's conviction draws forth the strength of the whole nation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In his old age he was diseased in his feet—even great kings face the wearing of years. Asa had reformed the land and won against enemies, yet time brings its own constraints. There is a humbling honesty in this detail.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Asa slept with his fathers in his father David's city, and Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his place. Another king falls asleep; another rises. The line continues, and the Lord's patience with His people stretches on.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nadab began to reign over Israel in the second year of Asa. While Judah has its moment of faithfulness, Israel's north spirals downward. The two kingdoms trace different paths; their fates remain bound.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He did that which was evil and walked in his father's way and in his sin—a king who repeats his father's error without asking why. To walk thoughtlessly in another's footsteps, good or ill, is to forfeit one's own soul.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Baasha conspired against Nadab and struck him at Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines. Gibbethon was a Levitical city; its mention echoes back through Israel's story. A conspiracy on holy ground—the betrayal cuts deeper.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Baasha killed him and reigned in his place. Another coup, another shift of power. The throne of Israel sits unsteady; no king's reign feels secure when the Lord is not consulted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Baasha struck all the house of Jeroboam and left none breathing. Total destruction—a purge that mirrors Yahweh's judgment through the prophet Ahijah. Yet Baasha commits it not in faith but in ambition. The same deed can fulfill the Lord's word without fulfilling the doer's heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: For the sins of Jeroboam which he sinned, and with which he made Israel to sin—the prophet's word stands. Jeroboam's idolatry set the north on a path of judgment. One king's choice ripples through all who follow, in blessing or in curse.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The rest of Nadab's acts—we are reminded again that what we see is not the whole. The chronicler selects; the Lord sees all. Our task is to trust what is recorded and hold the rest in humility.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: War between Asa and Baasha all their days—the kingdoms keep warring. Even as dynasties shift in Israel, the north and south remain enemies. The division of Solomon's kingdom casts a long shadow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Baasha reigned over all Israel in Tirzah for twenty-four years. Tirzah becomes the royal seat; it will be mentioned often hereafter. A city's name marks an era's center. The geography of power tells part of the story.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He did that which was evil and walked in the way of Jeroboam. Readers today hear an echo in this verse: how often we inherit patterns we do not question until the Lord shows us another way. Each generation must choose whether to break the chain or bind it tighter. Looking back from a longer road, I see how the Lord was always offering that choice—even then, even now.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
